title: 1054, told slowly
hookLine: a papal envoy lays a bull of excommunication on the altar of Hagia Sophia, and the break hardens

lines: A BULL LAID ON THE ALTAR.
cards: Constantinople, the great church of Hagia Sophia, and the liturgy is about to begin. Envoys from Rome walk up toward the altar, led by Cardinal Humbert.
He lays a document on the altar: a bull of excommunication against the city's patriarch, Michael Cerularius. Then the envoys walk out, shaking the dust from their feet.

By one account, one of the clergy runs after them and begs them to take it back. They refuse, and the document ends up on the floor. Soon after, the patriarch and his synod answer with an excommunication of their own.

teach.h: A LONG DRIFT, NOT A SINGLE SLAM.
teach.b: Told slowly, it's less a single slam than a long drift.
East and West had been growing apart: Greek and Latin, different customs at the altar, a dispute over wording in the creed, and the question of how far the authority of the bishop of Rome reaches.
Then that day in the great church. Notice what was excommunicated. Not whole churches.

The documents named people: the bull named the patriarch and those with him; the patriarch's synod answered against the envoys. The break hardened afterward, through later wounds this path will come to.
Scripture has a word for a split like this. In Mark, Jesus says no one sews new cloth onto an old garment, or, in the King James words, "the rent is made worse."
In Mark's Greek, that rent is a schisma, a tear in cloth. The church borrowed the word for its own tears.

teach.h: THAT THEY ALL MAY BE ONE.
teach.b: And the hope runs back to Jesus's prayer in John: "That they all may be one."

Much later, a pope, Paul the sixth, and a patriarch of Constantinople, Athenagoras, issued a joint statement regretting those old excommunications and wishing to remove them from the memory of the church.
Later still, Pope John Paul the second used a picture for East and West that became today's line: the church should breathe with both its lungs.

Catholics and Orthodox Christians still differ on real questions, and each church describes the division in its own terms. The Orthodox liturgy prays for the union of all. Catholics pray for unity too.
Both lungs, still learning to breathe together.

how: Catholic and Orthodox churches both pray for Christian unity in their services, and their leaders have met and issued joint statements, while still differing on questions such as the authority of the pope.

tear it up in front of everyone.
games.why: by one account, one of the clergy ran after them and pleaded. they refused, and the document ended up on the floor.

practice: Breathe all the way in and feel both sides of your chest rise, then breathe out, slowly, again and again. If you pray, pray Jesus's own line, that they all may be one, holding Catholic and Orthodox Christians together in mind.
If you don't, keep breathing, and notice two lungs working together without arguing over which one leads.

wordCard.voice: Schisma. The Greek word for a tear in cloth, borrowed for the slow-hardening split of ten fifty-four between East and West, with excommunications traded between envoys and a patriarch.

orig.note: Greek: a tear, a rent in cloth — the word in Mark 2:21, later used for a split in the church.

carryVoice: Your line: both lungs. A tear in cloth can still be mended. Day eight hundred eight.
